content: The FAT1 protocadherin is a protein in humans encoded by the FAT1 gene. This gene is an ortholog of the Drosophila fat gene, which encodes a tumor suppressor critical for regulating cell proliferation during Drosophila development. The FAT1 protein belongs to the cadherin superfamily, a group of integral membrane proteins characterized by cadherin-type repeats. The gene is highly expressed in various fetal epithelial tissues. Alternative splicing and promoter usage result in transcript variants, but these have not been fully characterized. In murine models, FAT1 knockout mice are not embryonically lethal, but the pups die within 48 hours due to abnormal fusion of podocyte foot processes in the kidney. These knockout mice also exhibit partially penetrant but often severe midline defects, including holoprosencephaly, microphthalmia-anophthalmia, and, in rare cases, cyclopia. The EVH motifs in the cytoplasmic tail of mouse FAT1 interact with Ena/VASP proteins, and RNAi-mediated ablation of FAT1 reduces cell migration in rat epithelial cells. The cytoplasmic tail of FAT1 also binds the transcriptional repressor Atrophin in rat vascular smooth muscle cells. At the carboxyl terminus of FAT1 lies a PDZ domain ligand motif (-HTEV). Zebrafish FAT1 has been shown to bind the protein Scribble and regulate Hippo signaling. In human SHSY5Y cells, a model for neuronal differentiation, FAT1 regulates Hippo kinase components, with FAT1 loss leading to nucleocytoplasmic relocation of TAZ and increased transcription of the Hippo target gene CTGF. The same study demonstrated that FAT1 also regulates TGF-beta signaling. Additionally, FAT1 binds beta-catenin and modulates Wnt signaling in colorectal cancer. The human FAT1 cadherin gene was cloned in 1995 from a human T-leukemia (T-ALL) cell line and consists of 27 exons located on chromosome 4q34–35. Structurally, the FAT1 protein is a single-pass transmembrane protein with an extracellular portion containing 34 cadherin repeats, 5 EGF-like domains, and a laminin-G-like domain. After translation, FAT1 undergoes furin-mediated S1 cleavage, forming a non-covalent heterodimer before being expressed on the cell surface. However, this processing is often disrupted in cancer cells, which express non-cleaved FAT1 on their surface. FAT1 cadherin is phosphorylated on its ectodomain, though this phosphorylation is not catalyzed by FJX1. The ectodomain of FAT1 can also be shed from the cell surface by the sheddase ADAM10, and the release of this ectodomain has been proposed as a potential biomarker in pancreatic cancer. FAT1 undergoes alternative splicing in breast cancer cells undergoing epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT), adding 12 amino acids to the cytoplasmic tail. Similar splice variants have been described in murine FAT1, where alternative splicing of the cytoplasmic tail regulates cell migration. The FAT1 cadherin has been implicated as both a putative tumor suppressor and an oncogene, depending on the context. Loss of heterozygosity for FAT1 has been reported in primary oral carcinomas and astrocytic tumors. Conversely, overexpression of FAT1 has been observed in various cancers, including ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) breast cancer, melanoma, and leukemia.
